title: Space Exploration
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Space Exploration Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Extreme environments, including space, require technology and adaptations: the effects of space on the body, satellites and telescopes, Canadian contributions such as the Canadarm, and life in extreme environments on Earth. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 6, Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 science worksheets (BC): Canadians in space, the Canadarm, satellites and telescopes, gravity in space, and living and working in space. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Technology lets people explore extreme places.
key_sub: Space has no air, extreme temperatures and radiation.
body_html:
How to think about it

Space is an extreme environment: there is no air to breathe, temperatures swing from very hot to very cold, and there is dangerous radiation. Astronauts need spacesuits and spacecraft that supply air, water and protection.

Canada has helped explore space with the Canadarm robotic arms, RADARSAT satellites and astronauts on the International Space Station. Satellites help with weather forecasts, GPS and communication; telescopes let us see far into space.

Example

Why do astronauts' muscles and bones weaken in space?

They do not have to work against gravity.

Answer: low gravity (microgravity)

Example

What did the Canadarm do?

A Canadian robot

Answer: moved cargo and helped build the space station

Common mistakes

  • Thinking there is no gravity at all on the space station (it is in free fall).
  • Thinking sound travels in space.
  • Forgetting how much space technology is used on Earth.

faq.q: What is an extreme environment on Earth?
faq.a: Places like the deep ocean, polar ice or hot springs, where living things need special adaptations.
They take images that show crop health, soil moisture and weather.

items.q: Why do stars look tiny?
c: They are smaller than the Moon.
items.e: Distance.

items.q: Which instrument lets you see craters on the Moon from your backyard?
items.e: Telescopes make faraway things look closer.

items.q: Why do astronauts exercise every day on the space station?
c: Without Earth's pull, their muscles and bones get weaker.
items.e: Exercise keeps them healthy.

items.q: Ava asks: “Why are planets round?”
c: Gravity pulls their material toward the centre from all sides.
items.e: Large bodies become round.

items.q: What does a space telescope like the James Webb Space Telescope do?
c: It sees faraway stars and galaxies without Earth's air in the way.
items.e: Canada built parts of the Webb telescope.

items.q: What is the Sun?
items.e: The closest star to Earth.

items.q: Priya asks: “Why does a comet speed up as it gets close to the Sun?”
c: The Sun's gravity pulls harder when the comet is closer.
items.e: Closer → stronger pull → faster.

items.q: What is a satellite?
c: an object that orbits a planet
items.e: The Moon is a natural satellite.

items.q: Ava asks: “Why is the Sun at the centre of our solar system's orbits?”
c: It was placed there by Jupiter.
It has more than 99% of the solar system's mass, so its gravity dominates.
items.e: Mass determines gravity.

items.q: Who was the first Canadian to command the International Space Station?
items.e: He commanded it in 2013.

items.q: Who was the first Canadian in space?
items.e: He flew in 1984.

items.q: What is the International Space Station?
c: a science lab that orbits Earth with astronauts on board
a rocket that goes to Mars
items.e: Canada is one of its partners.

items.q: Which is a use of artificial satellites?
c: weather forecasts, GPS and phone signals
items.e: Canada's RADARSAT satellites watch ice and forests.

items.q: Noah asks: “If a planet stopped moving forward, what would the Sun's gravity do?”
c: pull it straight toward the Sun
keep it in the same orbit
items.e: An orbit needs both forward motion and gravity.

items.q: Leah asks: “Why do moons orbit planets instead of flying off?”
c: The planet's gravity pulls on the moving moon.
items.e: Same idea at a smaller scale.

items.q: Which technology from space research is used on Earth?
items.e: Many inventions came from space research.

items.q: Is the Sun the biggest star in the Universe?
c: No. Many stars are much bigger than the Sun.
items.e: The Sun is a medium-sized star.

items.q: What is the Canadarm?
c: a robotic arm built in Canada and used on the space shuttle and space station
items.e: Canadarm2 is on the International Space Station.

items.q: Why are rockets launched with huge amounts of fuel?
c: They need a lot of thrust to escape Earth's gravity.
Because space is full of air
items.e: Leaving Earth takes a lot of energy.

items.q: Ethan asks: “If the Sun's gravity suddenly disappeared, what would Earth do?”
c: move off in a straight line into space
items.e: Without gravity's pull, nothing would curve Earth's path (Newton's first law).

items.q: Why does the sun look much brighter than other stars?
c: Other stars are turned off in the day.
It is the only star that gives off light.
It is much closer to Earth than any other star.
items.e: The sun is about 150 million km away. The next closest star is about 270000 times farther.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the left side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow B (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: What is a light-year?
c: the distance light travels in one year
the time it takes to see a star
items.e: A light-year is a distance: about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

items.q: Jeremy Hansen is part of which NASA mission to fly around the Moon?
items.e: He is the first Canadian on a Moon mission.

items.q: What do rovers on Mars do?
c: drive on the surface and study rocks, soil and air
items.e: Rovers are robots controlled from Earth.

items.q: Which statement about stars is true?
c: Stars are holes in the sky.
Stars are closer than the moon.
All stars are smaller than Earth.
Many stars are as big as or bigger than the sun.
items.e: Stars look like tiny dots only because they are so far away.

items.q: A person stands in Canada. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow A (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: How does distance change how bright a light looks?
c: The farther away, the dimmer it looks.
Lights look brightest from very far away.
The farther away, the brighter it looks.
items.e: Light spreads out as it travels, so less reaches your eyes from far away.

items.q: A person stands in Antarctica. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow A (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which is closest to Earth?
items.e: The sun is our closest star.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the right side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow D (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: A person stands at the South Pole. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the centre of Earth, so arrow C (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Why do astronauts float on the space station?
c: They and the station are falling around Earth together.
There is no gravity in space at all.
items.e: They are in constant free fall.

items.q: Why can't we see stars during the day?
c: The sun's bright light hides their dimmer light.
Stars move away during the day.
items.e: The stars are still there. Sunlight scattered in the sky outshines them.

items.q: A star looks very dim from Earth. Which could be true?
c: It must be smaller than a house.
It may be very far away.
It must not give off light.
items.e: Distance can make even a very bright star look dim.

items.q: Why do astronauts wear space suits on a spacewalk?
c: to give air and protect them from extreme temperatures and radiation
items.e: Space has no air to breathe.

items.q: What is one cost of space exploration?
c: It is very expensive and uses a lot of fuel.
items.e: People debate how to spend the money.

items.q: How did many Indigenous Peoples use the night sky?
c: to tell time, find directions and mark seasons
items.e: Star knowledge is passed down through stories.

items.q: Which object in the sky is a star?
items.e: The moon and planets reflect sunlight. The sun makes its own light.

items.q: What is space junk?
c: old satellites and pieces of rockets orbiting Earth
items.e: It can hit working satellites.

items.q: Two children drop a cup at the same time: one in Antarctica and one at a place on the right side of Earth. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
One falls up and one falls down.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: Why do astronauts on the space station exercise every day?
c: to make electricity for the station
in microgravity, bones and muscles weaken because they do not support the body's weight
items.e: Treadmills, bikes and resistance machines slow bone and muscle loss.

items.q: Why do some Indigenous knowledge keepers and scientists both study the night sky?
c: stars can be seen only from space
the sky has been used for navigation, calendars and stories for thousands of years
the sky only changes once a century
items.e: Many peoples used star patterns to mark seasons for hunting, fishing and planting.

items.q: Which body is the next major human destination planned by NASA's Artemis program, with Canadian participation?
items.e: Canada is building Canadarm3 for the Gateway station that will orbit the Moon.

items.q: What does the Canadarm do on a space station or shuttle?
c: it measures the temperature of the Sun
it makes oxygen for the crew
it is a robotic arm that moves equipment, catches spacecraft and helps astronauts
items.e: The Canadarm, Canadarm2 and Dextre are Canadian robotic systems used in space.

items.q: In Maya's model, a star has 2 times the mass of the Sun. A planet orbits it at the same distance as Earth. How does the pull on the planet compare with the Sun's pull on Earth (if the planets have equal mass)?
items.e: Gravity is proportional to mass.

items.q: In Benjamin's model, a planet moves to 4 times its distance from the Sun. What happens to the Sun's pull on it?
items.e: Gravity weakens with the square of distance: 4² = 16.

items.q: How can satellite data help farmers?
c: images show which parts of a field are dry, unhealthy or need fertilizer
satellites stop insects from eating crops
satellites make the growing season longer
items.e: This is called precision agriculture.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on the Earth is 10 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 80 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 80 × 10 = 800 N.

items.q: How do satellites help during forest fires and floods?
c: they stop the rain from falling
they map the area so emergency crews can see where help is needed
they put out the fires with water
items.e: Radar satellites such as Canada's RADARSAT can see through cloud and smoke.

items.q: What is one environmental concern about rocket launches?
c: they make the Moon move away
they release exhaust gases and particles into the atmosphere
items.e: Launches also add to space debris if stages are left in orbit.

items.q: Gravitational field strength on Venus is 8.9 N/kg. What is the weight there of an object with a mass of 40 kg?
items.e: weight = mass × g = 40 × 8.9 = 356 N.

items.q: Which technology uses signals from several satellites to find your position?
items.e: A receiver times signals from at least four satellites to work out its position.

items.q: Two children drop a rock at the same time: one in Antarctica and one on a ship at sea. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
One falls up and one falls down.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: What is a spin-off technology?
c: a satellite that spins to stay stable
a rocket that is used again
a product first developed for space that is later used on Earth
items.e: Examples include better water filters, memory foam and scratch-resistant lenses.

items.q: Two children drop a book at the same time: one at a place on the right side of Earth and one in Europe. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
One falls up and one falls down.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: Two children drop a ball at the same time: one on a ship at sea and one at a place on the right side of Earth. Which way does each one fall?
c: Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
One falls up and one falls down.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: Two children drop a rock at the same time: one at a place on the left side of Earth and one in Antarctica. Which way does each one fall?
c: One falls up and one falls down.
Both fall toward the centre of Earth.
Both fall toward the bottom of the page.
items.e: Down is toward Earth's centre everywhere, so both objects fall toward the ground under their feet.

items.q: On the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg), Olivia's backpack weighs 16 N. What is its mass?
items.e: mass = weight ÷ g = 16 ÷ 1.6 = 10 kg.

items.q: What is remote sensing?
c: listening to radio stations far away
measuring soil with a probe in the ground
collecting information about Earth from a distance, for example with satellite images
items.e: Satellites carry cameras and sensors that record light, heat and radar signals.

items.q: What can RADARSAT satellites see that ordinary cameras cannot?
c: the ground through clouds and darkness, using radar
items.e: Radar sends out microwaves and records the echoes, so it works day and night.

items.q: How do satellites help us study climate change?
c: they cool Earth by blocking sunlight
they measure ice cover, sea level, sea-surface temperature and greenhouse gases from orbit
they make rain fall over deserts
they remove carbon dioxide from the air
items.e: Remote sensing from orbit gives regular data for the whole planet.

items.q: What is mass?
c: the force of gravity on it
the amount of matter in an object
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Which quantity stays the same on the Moon as on the Earth: mass or weight?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What shape are most planetary orbits?
items.e: Slightly stretched circles.

items.q: What two things make an orbit?
c: forward motion and gravity pulling toward the centre
items.e: Gravity curves the path.

items.q: Which instrument on a satellite measures heat given off by the ground and oceans?
items.e: Warm objects give off infrared radiation, so the sensor can map temperatures.

items.q: What is space debris?
c: old satellites, rocket stages and fragments left in orbit
clouds of gas around the Sun
items.e: Even small pieces move at about 28 000 km/h and can damage working spacecraft.

items.q: Why do astronauts need spacesuits on a spacewalk?
c: the suits let them breathe the gases in space
the suits stop gravity from acting
space has no air to breathe, almost no pressure, extreme temperatures and strong radiation
items.e: The suit is a small spacecraft with its own air, pressure, cooling and radiation shield.

items.q: What does the size of gravitational attraction between two objects depend on?
c: their masses and the distance between them
items.e: More mass, closer: stronger.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge group of billions of stars held together by gravity
items.e: We live in the Milky Way.

items.q: Does Earth's gravity reach the Moon?
c: Yes. It keeps the Moon in orbit.
No, it stops at the atmosphere.
items.e: Gravity reaches far into space.

items.q: Which kind of orbit keeps a satellite above the same spot on the equator?
items.e: At about 36 000 km up, the satellite circles once a day, matching Earth's rotation.

items.q: How do communication satellites help remote northern communities?
c: they relay phone, internet and television signals where there are no cables
they melt snow on the roads
items.e: Many Arctic communities depend on satellite links for internet and health services.

items.q: Why is space debris a growing problem?
c: it blocks all sunlight from Earth
collisions make more pieces, which can damage satellites and the space station
items.e: More launches and collisions add to the debris; agencies track larger pieces.

items.q: What is the gravitational field strength on the Earth?
items.e: More precisely 9.8 N/kg.

items.q: What is a galaxy?
c: a huge system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity
items.e: The Milky Way has hundreds of billions of stars.

items.q: What unit is weight measured in?
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: What powers most satellites and the space station?
items.e: Sunlight is strong and constant in orbit, and the panels charge batteries for the dark part of each orbit.

items.q: Why do outer planets take longer to orbit the Sun?
c: They travel a longer path and move more slowly because the Sun's pull is weaker.
items.e: Distance matters.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Gravity pulls water down.”
c: Every dropped object in the class test fell to the floor, no matter where it was dropped.
A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
items.e: This observation directly shows that gravity pulls water down.

items.q: Why should students repeat a drop test several times?
c: to make sure the results are reliable
items.e: Repeated trials show whether the result happens every time.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Objects have weight because of gravity.”
c: A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
items.e: This observation directly shows that objects have weight because of gravity.

items.q: Which model best describes the solar system?
c: planets orbiting the Sun, held by the Sun's gravity
items.e: Sun-centered model.

items.q: Why would you weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
c: Your mass is less on the Moon.
The Moon's gravity is weaker because it has less mass.
There is no gravity on the Moon.
The Moon is closer to the Sun.
items.e: Weight depends on gravity.

items.q: Why do astronomers use light years and not kilometres?
c: It is a rule from the Moon.
Kilometres do not work in space.
The distances are so huge that kilometres give enormous numbers.
items.e: Convenient units.

items.q: Ethan drops two balls of the same size: a golf ball and a ping-pong ball, from 1 metre. They land at almost the same time. What does this show?
c: Heavier objects always fall much faster.
Gravity makes objects fall at about the same rate when air resistance is small.
Gravity does not affect light objects.
items.e: The pull of gravity speeds up all objects in the same way. Air resistance makes only a small difference here.

items.q: Which is the best way to show a younger student that “down” is toward Earth's centre?
c: Put toy figures all around a globe and point each one's arrow into the globe.
Drop a ball in the classroom only.
Draw an arrow to the bottom of a map.
items.e: A globe model shows that down points to the centre from every place.

items.q: Olivia's model shows a cloud of gas and dust shrinking and spinning faster. What forms at the centre?
items.e: Most mass collects at the centre.

items.q: When we look at a star 100 light years away, what are we seeing?
c: light that left the star 100 years ago
the star as it is right now
items.e: Looking back in time.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Gravity pulls toward Earth's centre.”
c: A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
Every dropped object in the class test fell to the floor, no matter where it was dropped.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
items.e: This observation directly shows that gravity pulls toward Earth's centre.

items.q: Ava swings a ball on a string in a circle. In her model, what does the string represent?
c: the Sun's gravity pulling the planet inward
items.e: Gravity is the inward pull.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “All objects fall toward the ground when dropped.”
c: Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
Every dropped object in the class test fell to the floor, no matter where it was dropped.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
items.e: This observation directly shows that all objects fall toward the ground when dropped.

items.q: Mateo measures that a ball dropped from 2 metres takes a little more than half a second to fall. What would happen if he did this in a different country?
c: It would fall about the same way, toward the ground there.
It would not fall at all.
items.e: Gravity works the same way everywhere on Earth's surface.

items.q: Ava drops a crumpled sheet of paper and a flat sheet from the same height. The crumpled one lands first. What variable did she change?
items.e: Both sheets have the same mass. Only the shape changed, which changes how much air slows the paper.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim: “Gravity acts without touching.”
c: A spring scale stretches when an object hangs from it.
A ball falls even though nothing touches it.
Plumb lines all over the world hang toward Earth's centre.
Rivers flow from mountains down to the sea.
items.e: This observation directly shows that gravity acts without touching.

items.q: If the Earth's axis were not tilted, what would happen?
c: There would be no day and night.
There would be almost no seasons.
Summer would last all year everywhere.
items.e: Tilt causes seasons.

items.q: Mei wants to test whether the height of a ramp changes how fast a car rolls down. What should she keep the same?
c: the car and the length and surface of the ramp
only the colour of the car
items.e: Only the height changes, so the test is fair.

items.q: Lucas lets go of the string while the ball is swinging. What does the ball do, and what does it model?
c: It falls straight down to the centre.
It flies off in a straight line, like a planet without gravity.
items.e: No inward pull, no curve.

items.q: Why would a spacecraft need more speed to orbit close to Jupiter than close to the Moon?
c: Jupiter is closer to the Sun.
Jupiter's much larger mass pulls harder.
items.e: More mass, more speed needed.
